p: Jesus walks out of the Temple right after saying God's house is left deserted.
b: The last words of chapter 23 are "your house is abandoned to you, deserted" (23:38). Now Jesus walks out and never teaches in the Temple again in Matthew. Ezekiel saw God's glory leave the Temple and stop on the mountain east of the city (Ezekiel 10:18–19; Ezekiel 11:23), which is the Mount of Olives. Many readers see Matthew drawing the same picture: the presence of God leaves the building, and judgment follows. Mark tells the same scene (Mark 13:1–2), and Luke sets the whole talk in the Temple itself (Luke 21:5–7).

p: One of the wonders of the Roman world, still being finished in Jesus' day.
b: Herod the Great began rebuilding the Temple about 20 BC, and work went on until about AD 63, only a few years before it was destroyed (John 2:20). Josephus says some of its white stones were about 25 cubits long (roughly 37 feet), and that from a distance the building looked like a snowy mountain covered in gold (Jewish War 5.5.6; Antiquities 15.11.3). Stones of the platform's walls still weigh many tons. The disciples were country men from Galilee, and the sight would have amazed them.

a: Every one will be knocked down
t: AD 70: the prediction and the event
p: In AD 70 Roman soldiers burned the Temple and pulled the city down.
b: After a siege of more than four months, Titus's army burned the Temple at the end of August AD 70. Josephus, who watched, says Titus then ordered the whole city and Temple torn down, leaving only three towers and part of the city wall on the west side, as a camp for the garrison and to show how strong the place had been (Jewish War 7.1.1). That was part of the city wall. The Western Wall in Jerusalem today is something else, part of the Temple platform's retaining wall, not the Temple building, so it does not contradict the saying. Critical scholars often date Matthew after 70 partly because of this saying. Others answer that Jeremiah and Micah had already foretold the Temple's fall (Jeremiah 7:14; Micah 3:12), and that a prophet could say it again.

a: not one stone will be left on a stone
p: The rabbis also grieved and asked why the Second Temple fell.
b: For Jews the burning of the Temple was the great disaster of the age, and it is still mourned on the fast of Tisha B'Av with the reading of Lamentations. The rabbis gave their own answer to why it happened: the first Temple fell for idolatry, sexual sin and bloodshed, but the second fell because of "hatred without cause" among Jews, even though people studied the law and did kind deeds (Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 9b). Jesus' words stand in a line of Jewish prophets who warned their own people from within. Later Christian use of this passage to say that God rejected the Jews goes far beyond what Jesus or Matthew says.

t: Sitting on the Mount of Olives
p: The hill where Zechariah saw the LORD stand on the day of judgment.
b: The Mount of Olives rises east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley, and from it one looks straight across at the Temple (Mark 13:3 says he sat "opposite the Temple"). Zechariah 14:4 says, "His feet will stand, on that day, on the Mount of Olives." Jesus sits, as a teacher does, as he did before the Sermon on the Mount (5:1). Matthew's first and last great talks are both given on a mountain. In Acts 1:11–12 the angels promise that he will come back in the same way, and the disciples return to the city from this hill.

p: The disciples ask about the Temple and about the end. Did they think these were one event?
b: "This" points back to the Temple's fall (24:2). "Your coming and the completion of the age" points forward. Many interpreters think the disciples assumed the two were one event, and that Jesus' answer gradually pulls them apart. How the answer divides is the key question of the chapter. Full preterists (J. Stuart Russell, Max King) read all of chapters 24–25, the judgment included, as fulfilled in AD 70. Partial preterists (R. T. France, R. C. Sproul, Kenneth Gentry) read 24:4–35 as AD 70 and see a turn at 24:36, from "those days" to "that day," the final return. Futurists read most of the chapter as still to come. Historicists trace its signs through church history; idealists see a pattern for every age; and a double-fulfillment reading (Chrysostom, Calvin) sees AD 70 and the end told together. Mark 13:4 asks when "these things" will be and what sign will show they are about to be accomplished; Matthew names "your coming" and "the completion of the age."

p: The word for an emperor's state visit. Only Matthew among the Gospels uses it.
b: Parousia means presence or arrival. In Greek letters and inscriptions it was used for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city, with crowds going out to meet him. Paul uses it for Jesus' return (1 Thessalonians 4:15; 1 Corinthians 15:23). Among the Gospels only Matthew has it, four times, all in this chapter (24:3, 27, 37, 39). Jehovah's Witnesses translate it "presence" and teach an invisible presence that began in 1914; most churches read it as Christ's visible return.

p: The KJV's "end of the world" hides that this is about the close of an age.
b: The Greek is synteleia tou aiōnos, "the completion of the age." The KJV says "the end of the world," which suggests the planet blowing up. Jews spoke of "this age" and "the age to come": the present time of evil and the time when God puts things right. Matthew uses the phrase five times (13:39, 40, 49; 24:3; 28:20). Preterists note that Hebrews 9:26 says Christ appeared "at the completion of the ages," so an age could end in the first century. Others take it as the close of history at Christ's return.

p: Josephus names men who promised signs and freedom in the years before the war.
b: Josephus tells of Theudas, who led crowds to the Jordan promising to split it (Antiquities 20.5.1; Acts 5:36), and of "the Egyptian," who led a crowd from the wilderness to the Mount of Olives (Jewish War 2.13.5) and promised that the city walls would fall at his command (Antiquities 20.8.6; Acts 21:38). Josephus says 30,000 followed him; Acts says 4,000. During the war, Simon bar Giora acted like a king. Josephus calls such men false prophets and impostors, not messiahs, so the exact title is not recorded. In AD 132 Simon bar Kosiba was hailed as Bar Kokhba, "son of the star," by Rabbi Akiva. Futurists expect the warning to be fulfilled again before the end.

t: The years before the end of the Temple
p: Rome's civil war of AD 68–69 shook the whole empire.
b: In the years leading up to AD 70 the Jewish revolt began (66), Nero died (68), and four emperors ruled in one year (69) as Roman armies fought each other. Tacitus opens his history of these years by calling it a time "rich in disasters, terrible with battles, torn by civil strife" (Histories 1.2). Preterists see these verses fulfilled then. Jesus' point, though, is that wars are not the sign: "the end is not here yet."

p: The first century had both; every century since has too.
b: Acts 11:28 records a great famine under Claudius (about AD 46–48). Laodicea was shaken by an earthquake in AD 60 (Tacitus, Annals 14.27), and Pompeii was damaged in AD 62. Revelation's first four seals show the same list of war, famine and death (Revelation 6:1–8). Futurists often say such events will increase in frequency before the end; others note that Jesus calls them only the beginning, and warns against reading them as a timetable.

a: the start of the labor pains
t: The birth pains of the Messiah
p: A Jewish picture: suffering before the new age is born.
b: The prophets compared the coming of God's new age to a woman in labor (Isaiah 26:17–19; Isaiah 66:7–9; Micah 4:9–10). Later rabbis spoke of "the birth pains of the Messiah," troubles before his coming, and some prayed not to live to see them (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 98b). Paul uses the image too (1 Thessalonians 5:3; Romans 8:22), and Revelation 12:2 shows a woman crying out in labor. Labor pains hurt, but they mean a birth is near.
r: Isaiah 26:17–19; Isaiah 66:7–9; Micah 4:9–10; 1 Thessalonians 5:3; Romans 8:22; Revelation 12:2

p: The same word as "great suffering" in 24:21 and Revelation 7:14.
b: Thlipsis means pressure, crushing, distress. Older English Bibles say "tribulation." This site renders it "suffering," as in Revelation (Revelation 1:9; Revelation 7:14), so readers can see the same word return in 24:21 and 24:29. "Hand over" is the word used for Judas betraying Jesus and for Jesus being handed over to death (26:2). Matthew has already given most of these warnings when Jesus sent out the Twelve (10:17–22).

p: To be tripped up: to lose faith and fall away.
b: The verb skandalizō means to cause someone to stumble, from skandalon, the trigger of a trap. Matthew uses it for people who lose their faith when trouble comes (13:21) and for the disciples on the night Jesus is arrested (26:31). Here the danger is not only outside persecution but believers turning on each other.

p: Lawlessness: living as if God's law did not count.
b: Anomia is Matthew's word for those who ignore God's law while seeming religious (7:23; 13:41; 23:28). Love grows cold when people stop treating others the way the law requires. Revelation 2:4 warns the church at Ephesus that it has left the love it had at first.

t: Preached to the whole world: done or not yet?
p: Oikoumenē often meant the Roman world. Was this fulfilled before AD 70?
b: Oikoumenē, "inhabited world," is the word Luke uses for Augustus' census of "the whole world" (Luke 2:1). Preterists point to Paul, who said in the 50s and early 60s that the good news was bearing fruit "in the whole world" (Colossians 1:6, 23; Romans 1:8; Romans 10:18), so the end of 24:14 could be AD 70. Futurists say every people group must hear first, and many mission movements took this verse as their motto. Idealists read it as the task of the church in every age.

t: What is the abomination of desolation?
p: Daniel's horror in the Temple. Antiochus, Roman soldiers, the Zealots, or a future Antichrist?
b: Daniel speaks of a disgusting thing that leaves the sanctuary desolate (Daniel 9:27; Daniel 11:31; Daniel 12:11). Matthew's Greek, to bdelygma tēs erēmōseōs, is the Septuagint's rendering of Daniel's Hebrew shiqquts (me)shomem, "the detestable thing that desolates." 1 Maccabees 1:54 uses the phrase for the pagan altar Antiochus IV set up in 167 BC. Jesus speaks of it as still to come. Readings: Roman armies and standards: Luke's parallel says "When you see Jerusalem being encircled by army camps" (Luke 21:20), and Josephus says soldiers set up their standards in the Temple court and sacrificed to them (Jewish War 6.6.1). The Zealots, who turned the Temple into a fortress and shed blood in it in 67–68 (Jewish War 4.3). A future Antichrist who sits in a rebuilt temple (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4), the futurist view. Idealists see any power that takes God's place.
r: Daniel 9:27; Daniel 11:31; Daniel 12:11; 1 Maccabees 1:54; Luke 21:20; Mark 13:14; 2 Thessalonians 2:3–4

p: No "the" in Greek: the Temple, or the holy land?
b: Matthew writes en topō hagiō with no article. Most read it as the Temple. Some preterists take it more widely as holy ground, the land or the city, which fits Luke's armies around Jerusalem. Mark has "standing where he must not stand" with a masculine "he" (Mark 13:14), as if the horror is a person, which futurists stress.

a: the one who reads this should think about what it means
t: Who is speaking to "the one who reads"?
p: A note to readers of Daniel, or to readers of the Gospel?
b: Jesus is speaking, yet the words address a reader. Some think Jesus means the reader of Daniel: study the prophecy. Most scholars think the Gospel writer speaks to his own readers, as Mark does (Mark 13:14), perhaps hinting at something dangerous to name openly, such as Rome. The aside shows the passage was meant to be read aloud and pondered in the churches.

p: Eusebius says the Jerusalem church fled before the war.
b: Eusebius writes that the church in Jerusalem, warned by a revelation, left the city before the war and settled in Pella, a town east of the Jordan (Church History 3.5.3). Epiphanius tells the same story later. Some scholars doubt it, since Pella is in the lowlands, not the hills, and Gentile towns like Pella were attacked by Jewish rebels in 66. Many accept a real core. Either way, the advice fits a real war: get out of Judea, do not shelter in the city.

p: Houses had flat roofs reached by outside stairs.
b: Village houses had flat roofs of beams and packed earth, used for drying crops, sleeping in summer and praying (Acts 10:9). Stairs ran up the outside, so a person could flee without going back in. The point of 24:17–18 is speed: leave everything.

p: Only Matthew adds the Sabbath, a sign his readers still kept it.
b: Mark 13:18 has only "in winter." Matthew adds "or on a Sabbath," which suggests his Jewish-Christian readers still kept the Sabbath and would find fleeing on it a real problem. Jewish practice allowed saving a life on the Sabbath, but long travel was limited, gates might be shut, and supplies could not be bought. Winter was the rainy season, when the wadis flooded. Josephus tells of refugees from Gadara trapped against the swollen Jordan in the spring of 68 (Jewish War 4.7.5).

p: Daniel's "time of distress": AD 70, a future seven years, or the whole church age?
b: The words echo Daniel 12:1, a time of distress unlike any since nations began. Josephus, in words much like these, wrote that the misfortunes of all peoples since the world began seemed small next to what the Jews suffered in this war (Jewish War, preface 4), and he counts more than a million dead in the siege (6.9.3), a number many think too high. Preterists read 24:21 as that siege. Futurists expect a future great tribulation, often the last seven years of Daniel 9:27. Idealists see the suffering of God's people in every age. Revelation 7:14 speaks of those who "have come out of the great suffering."

a: no one at all would be saved
t: "Saved": rescued alive, or saved for good?
p: The same verb as 24:13. It can mean physical rescue or final salvation.
b: The Greek is ouk an esōthē pasa sarx, "no flesh would be saved." Sōzō can mean being rescued from death, as when the disciples cry "Lord, save us!" in a storm (8:25), or being saved for God's kingdom. Many versions translate it "no one would survive," taking it of the siege, which suits the preterist reading. The Plain keeps "saved" so readers can see the link with 24:13, "whoever holds out to the end, that person will be saved," which futurist and other readers take of final salvation.

a: for the sake of the chosen
p: God's people: the church, or Israel during a future tribulation?
b: "The chosen" (eklektoi, the elect) appear in 24:22, 24 and 31. Most readers take them to be Jesus' followers. Dispensational writers such as Walvoord read them here as chosen Israel, saved through a future tribulation. Preterists note that the Romans ended the siege in five months; without that, they say, no one in Judea would have survived.

p: Moses warned that a false prophet's miracle proves nothing.
b: Deuteronomy 13:1–3 says that even if a prophet's sign comes true, he must not be followed if he leads people to other gods. Paul says the lawless one will come with false signs and wonders (2 Thessalonians 2:9), and in Revelation the beast from the land "performs great signs" and "deceives those who live on the earth" (Revelation 13:13–14). Josephus tells how, as the Temple burned, a false prophet told a crowd to go up to the Temple to receive signs of rescue, and they died in the fire (Jewish War 6.5.2).

p: Deliverers led crowds into the desert, where Israel's story began.
b: Israel was born in the wilderness, and many expected the final rescue to begin there too (Isaiah 40:3; Hosea 2:14). The Egyptian led his followers "into the wilderness" (Acts 21:38), and Josephus tells of others who promised signs in the desert (Jewish War 2.13.4). "Back rooms" means a secret hiding place. Jesus says his coming will not need rumors: no one will have to go looking.

a: Lightning flashes out in the east
p: Sudden, public and impossible to miss.
b: Lightning is seen across the whole sky at once. The contrast is with the secret messiahs of 24:26: the true coming will not be hidden in a room. Some preterists read the coming here as Christ coming in judgment through Rome's armies, which marched from the east; most readers take it as his final return, seen by all (Revelation 1:7).

p: Aetos usually means eagle. Rome's legions marched under eagle standards.
b: The Greek aetoi normally means eagles, though it could be used for vultures, which gather at a dead body (Job 39:27–30). The saying sounds like a proverb: where there is a carcass, birds will find it, so the end will be obvious. Some preterists hear a pointed meaning: the eagle was the standard of every Roman legion, gathering over a dead Jerusalem. Revelation 19:17–18 calls the birds to "the great supper of God."

t: "Right after": the hardest word in the chapter
p: Euthéōs, "immediately." How can the coming follow right after AD 70?
b: If 24:15–28 describes AD 70, then the sun going dark and the Son of Man's coming follow "immediately" after it. Readers solve this in different ways. Preterists say 24:29–31 is also AD 70, told in the prophets' picture language for the fall of a nation. Futurists say all of 24:15–31 is future, so there is no gap. Others say prophets saw near and far events together, like mountain peaks seen from a distance. Some critical scholars, following Albert Schweitzer, conclude that Jesus or Matthew expected the end to follow the war at once.

p: The prophets' language for God judging a nation.
b: The lines mix Isaiah 13:10, about the fall of Babylon, and Isaiah 34:4, about Edom, with Joel 2:10. In those prophecies the sky going dark describes the end of a kingdom, not the end of the universe. "The stars will fall" follows the Greek of Isaiah 34:4, where the stars fall like leaves; the Hebrew says the host of heaven will rot away. Revelation's sixth seal uses the same pictures: "The sun became black ... The stars of the sky fell to the earth" (Revelation 6:12–13). Literal readers expect real signs in the sky; others hear the collapse of a world order.
r: Isaiah 13:10; Isaiah 34:4; Ezekiel 32:7–8; Joel 2:10; Joel 2:31; Amos 8:9; Revelation 6:12–13; Acts 2:20

a: the sign of the Son of Man
p: The Son himself? A banner? Early Christians said a cross in the sky.
b: The disciples asked for a sign (24:3). Here it comes, but it is not explained. Some take it to mean that the Son of Man himself is the sign. Others think of the banner and trumpet that call the exiles home (Isaiah 11:12; Isaiah 18:3; Isaiah 27:13). The Didache (16:6) lists "a sign spread out in heaven," then a trumpet, then the resurrection. Cyril of Jerusalem taught that it would be a shining cross (Catechetical Lectures 15.22), a view many church fathers shared.

a: all the tribes of the earth will mourn
p: Revelation 1:7 joins the same two prophecies: Zechariah 12 and Daniel 7.
b: Zechariah 12:10–14 says the families of the land will mourn for the one they pierced, each tribe by itself. Matthew alone among the Gospels adds this line here. Revelation 1:7 says, "All the tribes of the earth will mourn over him," combining it with Daniel 7:13 just as Matthew does. The Greek gē can mean "earth" or "land," so preterists read the tribes of the land of Israel mourning in AD 70; others read every people on earth, mourning in repentance or in fear.

a: coming on the clouds of the sky
p: In Daniel the one like a son of man comes to God's throne to receive a kingdom.
b: Daniel 7:13–14 sees "one like a son of man" coming with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days, and he is given rule over all peoples. In Daniel the movement is toward God. Matthew's "on the clouds" (epi tōn nephelōn) matches the Old Greek of Daniel 7:13; the Aramaic has "with the clouds" (ʿim ʿanane), as does Theodotion's Greek and Mark 14:62. N. T. Wright and R. T. France read Jesus' words as his vindication and enthronement, shown when the Temple fell; Jesus tells the high priest he will see this "from now on" (26:64). Most Christians through history, and most futurists, read it as Jesus' visible return to earth (Acts 1:11; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). Revelation 14:14 shows "someone like a son of man" sitting on a cloud.

t: The great trumpet and the four winds
p: Isaiah's great trumpet calls the scattered exiles home.
b: Isaiah 27:13 says a great trumpet will be blown and the lost in Assyria and Egypt will come to worship in Jerusalem. Zechariah 2:6 speaks of God's people scattered "to the four winds," and Deuteronomy 30:4 promises to gather them from the ends of the sky. Paul hears a trumpet at the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:52; 1 Thessalonians 4:16), and Revelation's seventh trumpet announces the kingdom (Revelation 11:15). Some preterists take "angels" in its basic sense, "messengers," and read this as missionaries gathering the nations after AD 70.
r: Isaiah 27:13; Zechariah 2:6; Deuteronomy 30:4; 1 Corinthians 15:52; 1 Thessalonians 4:16; Revelation 11:15; Revelation 7:1

p: Unlike the evergreen olive, the fig loses its leaves in winter and buds again in spring.
b: Unlike the olive and other evergreens, the fig drops its leaves in winter and puts out new ones in spring, so commentators point out that its new leaves are a clear sign that summer is near (Mark 11:13 has a fig tree in leaf at Passover). In Hebrew "summer" (qayits) sounds like "end" (qets), the pun behind Amos 8:1–2; Jesus may be using it. Dispensational writers such as Hal Lindsey read the fig tree as the nation of Israel, reborn in 1948. Most scholars see only a lesson from nature. Jesus had cursed a fig tree near the Temple just days before (21:18–22).
r: Amos 8:1–2; 21:18–22; Mark 11:13; Luke 21:29–31; Song of Songs 2:11–13; Revelation 6:13

p: The Greek verb has no subject: "it is near" or "he is near."
b: Engys estin can mean "it is near" (the end, or the kingdom) or "he is near" (the Son of Man). Luke 21:31 has "the kingdom of God is near," which supports "it." The picture of someone "at the doors" may suggest a person (James 5:9; Revelation 3:20). The Plain follows "it," as the KJV does; many modern versions have "he." The verb "know" can also be a command: "know that it is near."

p: C. S. Lewis called it the most embarrassing verse in the Bible. Readings differ widely.
b: Elsewhere in Matthew "this generation" means Jesus' own hearers (11:16; 12:41–45; 23:36, "it will all fall on this generation"). Readings: Jesus' contemporaries, with "all these things" fulfilled in AD 70, about forty years later (preterists, R. T. France, N. T. Wright). The generation that sees the signs, at the end (many futurists; Hal Lindsey linked it to Israel's rebirth in 1948). The Jewish people as a race, which will last until the end (the Scofield Reference Bible). Human beings, or the unbelieving kind. Jesus was mistaken, the view of Albert Schweitzer; C. S. Lewis, a believer, called the verse "the most embarrassing" in the Bible and still trusted Jesus because he also said he did not know the day (24:36).

a: my words will never be gone
p: Jesus claims for his words what Scripture says of God's word.
b: Isaiah 40:8 says the grass withers but the word of our God stands forever, and Psalm 102:25–27 says heaven and earth will wear out but God remains. Jesus had said the Law would last until heaven and earth pass away (5:18). Now he says his own words will outlast them.

a: As for that day and hour
p: "As for" (peri de) often begins a new topic. Is this where Jesus turns from AD 70 to his return?
b: Up to 24:35 Jesus speaks of "those days" with signs that can be seen. From 24:36 he speaks of "that day," which no one can know and which comes without warning, like the flood. Many partial preterists and other interpreters (R. T. France, among others) see the break here: 24:4–35 answers "when will this happen?" and 24:36–25:46 answers "your coming and the completion of the age." Futurists usually read the whole chapter as one future sequence. The Greek peri de, "now about," is how Paul turns to new questions (1 Corinthians 7:1; 1 Corinthians 8:1).

t: How can the Son not know?
p: The church fathers argued over this verse for centuries.
b: Arians in the 300s used this verse to argue that the Son was less than the Father. Athanasius answered that Christ did not know as a human being, since he truly took on human limits, though as God he knew all things (Orations against the Arians 3.42–46). Gregory of Nazianzus said the same (Oration 30.15). Augustine suggested that the Son "did not know" in the sense of not making it known (On the Trinity, book 1). Many modern Christians point to Philippians 2:7, where the Son "emptied himself." Some scribes simply left "nor the Son" out (see the variant).

p: Not the wickedness of Noah's day, but its everyday carelessness.
b: Genesis 6:5 describes the evil of that generation, but Jesus stresses something else: people were simply going about their lives, eating, drinking and holding weddings, until the very day "Noah went into the ark" (Genesis 7:7). The danger is not that the signs are hard to read but that people stop expecting anything. Luke 17:26–30 adds the days of Lot. Peter also uses the flood as a picture of judgment (1 Peter 3:20; 2 Peter 3:5–7).

p: The flood "carried off" (airō); in 24:40 one is "taken along" (paralambanō).
b: In 24:39 the flood ēren, "took away, swept off," everyone outside the ark. In 24:40–41 a different verb is used, paralambanetai, "is taken along," the word for Joseph taking Mary home (1:20, 24) and Jesus taking disciples with him (17:1; John 14:3). Readers who see a rapture in 24:40 stress the second verb; readers who think those "taken" are taken in judgment stress the link with the flood.

a: One is taken along, and one is left behind
p: The famous rapture verse. Is it better to be taken or to be left?
b: Pre-tribulation rapture: believers are caught up to meet Christ (1 Thessalonians 4:17) while others are left behind. This is how much popular pre-tribulation teaching reads the verse, including the Left Behind novels by the pre-tribulation teacher Tim LaHaye and Jerry Jenkins. Many dispensational scholars, however, apply the passage to the end of the tribulation, not to the rapture (Louis Barbieri in The Bible Knowledge Commentary; John Walvoord). Taken in judgment: as the flood "carried them all off" (24:39), so the one taken is removed in judgment and the one left survives; in Luke 17:37 the disciples ask "Where, Lord?" and hear about vultures and a body (Barbieri and other dispensational writers; some non-dispensational scholars agree). Taken to be with Christ at his one return: the angels gather the chosen (24:31) when he comes after the tribulation, as most churches teach. Either way the point is that two people side by side will meet very different ends.

p: Women ground the family's flour each morning, often two at one mill.
b: A hand mill was two round stones; one woman, or two facing each other, turned the upper stone to grind grain for the day's bread (Exodus 11:5). It was ordinary daily work, which is the point. Codex Bezae and several Old Latin manuscripts add here the line about two in one bed from Luke 17:34, as Tischendorf's apparatus reports.

a: dig his way into the house
p: Houses of mud brick: a thief dug through the wall.
b: Many houses had walls of mud brick or rubble, so burglars dug through rather than picking a lock (Exodus 22:2; Job 24:16; Ezekiel 12:5). The Greek verb means "dig through." A "watch" was a part of the night: Romans counted four watches of about three hours (14:25).

p: This saying became one of the best-known images in the New Testament.
b: Paul writes that the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night (1 Thessalonians 5:2), and so does 2 Peter 3:10. In Revelation the risen Jesus says, "I will come like a thief" (Revelation 3:3), and "Look, I am coming like a thief!" (Revelation 16:15). The image is about surprise, not about stealing.

a: an hour you are not counting on
p: The chapter gives signs, then says the coming is unexpected. How do these fit?
b: Jesus lists signs (24:4–33) and then says the hour comes when no one expects it (24:36–44). Some solve this by dividing the chapter into two events: the Temple's fall, which had signs, and the final coming, which has none (partial preterists, France). Pre-tribulation futurists divide it into a signless rapture and a later coming after signs. Others say the signs mark the whole age and never let anyone set a date. All agree on the practical point: be ready now.

p: Leaders who feed God's household, or every disciple?
b: The slave is put over the other slaves to give them food at the right time. Many read this as a word to church leaders, who must feed God's people while the master is away; in Luke 12:41–42 Peter asks whether the story is for the disciples or for everyone. Others apply it to every believer. In Matthew's community the warning against beating fellow slaves (24:49) fits leaders who abuse their position.

p: The parables of 24:45–25:30 all imagine a master who takes a long time.
b: The evil slave says his master is delayed (24:48); the groom is delayed (25:5); the master of the talents returns after "much time" (25:19). Many scholars think Matthew's church was already asking why Jesus had not yet returned, the question 2 Peter 3:4 answers. The parables say delay is no excuse: it is the time to be faithful.

p: A savage punishment, or an idiom for being cut off?
b: Dichotomeō means to cut in two. Cutting a person in pieces was a known punishment (1 Samuel 15:33; Hebrews 11:37). But the slave then receives a share with the hypocrites, which suggests he is still alive. Some scholars think an Aramaic idiom for "cut off" from the community lies behind it; the Qumran Community Rule says a false member will be cut off from among the sons of light (1QS 2:16–17).

a: There people will weep and grind their teeth.
p: Matthew's refrain for final loss, found six times.
b: Only Matthew uses this refrain so often (8:12; 13:42, 50; 22:13; 24:51; 25:30). Grinding the teeth can show rage (Psalm 35:16; Psalm 112:10) or bitter pain. Matthew uses vivid pictures, outer darkness and fire, for the loss of God's kingdom.

p: "Virgins" in older Bibles: young unmarried girls, here the bride's attendants.
b: Parthenos means a girl of marriageable age who is not yet married. The KJV's "virgins" is accurate, but the story is not about sexual purity. These are the bride's friends, waiting to welcome the groom and walk with him in the wedding procession. Ten was a common number for a group (Ruth 4:2).

p: Lampades may be torches: sticks wrapped in oil-soaked rags.
b: Lampas can mean a small clay oil lamp, but more often a torch. Joachim Jeremias argued that these were poles topped with rags soaked in oil, which burned only about fifteen minutes and needed fresh oil before the procession, so the foolish girls' torches were "going out" as soon as they were lit. At village weddings the groom came at night, often late after bargaining over the bride's gifts, to bring the bride from her father's house to his own home, and the guests lit his way.

p: God as Israel's husband; Jesus as the groom; the Lamb's wedding.
b: The prophets pictured God as the husband of his people (Isaiah 54:5; Isaiah 62:5; Hosea 2:16–20). Jesus calls himself the groom (9:15), and John the Baptist calls himself the groom's friend (John 3:29). Revelation ends with the Lamb's wedding: "the wedding of the Lamb has come, ... and his wife has made herself ready" (Revelation 19:7), and the holy city comes down "made ready like a bride" (Revelation 21:2). In 25:1 the word for "meet" is hypantēsis; in 25:6, "Go out and meet him," it is apantēsis, the word Paul uses for meeting the Lord in the air (1 Thessalonians 4:17), a word for going out to escort an arriving guest.
r: 9:15; 25:6; John 3:29; Isaiah 62:5; Hosea 2:16–20; Revelation 19:7–9; Revelation 21:2; 1 Thessalonians 4:17; 22:1–14

p: The same pair as the two builders at the end of the Sermon on the Mount.
b: Phronimos means practical, thinking ahead. It is the word for the sensible man who built on rock and the foolish man who built on sand (7:24–27), and for the faithful slave (24:45). Matthew's first and last long talks both end by dividing people into the sensible and the foolish.

p: Good works, the Holy Spirit, faith, love? Readers have long disagreed.
b: Jesus does not say. John Chrysostom took the oil to be mercy and giving to the poor, without which even a life of virginity is useless (Homilies on Matthew 78). Many Protestant and Pentecostal preachers take it as the Holy Spirit, or a living faith, since oil often stands for the Spirit's anointing (1 Samuel 16:13). Others say the story only means "be prepared" and the oil need not stand for anything. In Matthew, being ready usually means doing the Father's will (7:21) and acts of mercy (25:31–46).

p: The sensible ones fell asleep too. Sleep is not the failure.
b: No one is blamed for sleeping; all ten slept. The difference is what they had prepared before they slept. Yet the story ends "So stay awake" (25:13). Most readers conclude that "staying awake" means being ready, not never resting.

a: There might not be enough for us and for you
p: It sounds selfish. Many hear a point about what cannot be borrowed.
b: Elsewhere Jesus praises giving to anyone who asks (5:42). Here the sensible girls refuse. The story is not about sharing; it shows that readiness for the groom cannot be handed over at the last minute. Each person must be ready for himself or herself.

p: As at the flood, the door is shut and the time for getting in is over.
b: In Genesis 7:16, "the LORD shut the door behind" Noah. Jesus has just compared his coming to the flood (24:37–39). The shut door appears in Luke's teaching too (Luke 13:24–25). The wedding feast is a common picture of the kingdom of God (8:11; 22:1–14; Revelation 19:9).

t: "Lord, Lord ... I do not know you"
p: An echo of the end of the Sermon on the Mount.
b: In 7:21–23 many say "Lord, Lord" and hear "I never knew you." Here the latecomers say the same and hear "I do not know you" (25:12). In both places, calling Jesus Lord is not enough without doing what the Father wants. A guest speaking to a groom might simply say "Sir, sir"; the Plain keeps "Lord, Lord" on purpose so the echo of 7:21–22 stays visible.

p: Luke tells a similar story with a nobleman, ten slaves and smaller sums.
b: In Luke 19:11–27 a nobleman goes to a far country to receive a kingdom, gives ten slaves one mina each (about four months' wages), and his citizens send word that they do not want him as king. That detail recalls Archelaus, Herod's son, who went to Rome in 4 BC to be confirmed as king while a Jewish delegation opposed him (Josephus, Antiquities 17.11.1). Luke tells the story because people thought the kingdom would appear at once. Scholars debate whether these are two stories Jesus told or one story retold.

t: A talent was money, not a skill
p: The English word "talent," meaning a gift or ability, comes from this parable.
b: A talent (talanton) was a weight of silver, about 6,000 denarii. A denarius was a laborer's pay for a day (20:2), so one talent was close to twenty years' wages, and five talents was a fortune. In 18:24 a slave owes ten thousand talents. English "talent" came to mean a natural gift because medieval readers took the parable as being about using God-given abilities. The master gives "to each according to what he could handle," so the talents and the abilities are different things.

p: The Greek "immediately" can go with the master leaving or with the slave going to work.
b: Old Greek manuscripts had no punctuation. The KJV, following its Greek, says the master "straightway took his journey." Modern editions, including the SBL and NA28, put a period after "left the country" and read "right away" with the first slave, who loses no time. The Plain follows the modern editions.

p: The safe way to guard money, according to Jewish law.
b: With no banks for ordinary people, burying money was common (13:44). The rabbis held that a man who buried money left with him was not liable if it was stolen, because "money can only be guarded in the ground" (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 42a). So the third slave did the legally safe thing. In Luke the slave wraps the money in a cloth (Luke 19:20), which by the same rule was careless. The master's anger shows he wanted more than safety: he wanted the money used.

a: Come in to your master's joy!
p: Chara means joy, but may point to a feast.
b: Chara is joy. Some scholars think it here means the celebration itself, the master's feast, as joy and banquet go together in Jewish speech. Either way, the reward for faithful work is more responsibility and a share in the master's own happiness.

p: Most read the master as Christ; some read the third slave as a hero.
b: The traditional reading: the master is Christ, who will return, and the third slave's fear comes from a false picture of him; he is judged by his own words (25:26). A minority reading, argued by William Herzog, sees the master as a greedy rich man who profits from others' work, and the third slave as a whistle-blower who refuses to join the exploitation. Matthew's setting, between the ten young women and the final judgment, points strongly to the first reading, but the second reminds readers how a peasant audience might have heard a story about a harsh lender.

a: you collect where you never scattered
p: Sowing seed, or winnowing grain?
b: The verb diaskorpizō means "scatter." Some take it as a second picture of sowing; many commentators think of winnowing, when grain was tossed into the wind so the chaff scattered and the kernels could be gathered. Either way the master profits from work he did not do himself.

p: The Torah forbade lending at interest to a fellow Israelite.
b: Exodus 22:25 and Deuteronomy 23:19–20 forbid charging interest to a fellow Israelite, though it was allowed with foreigners. In the Greek and Roman world, bankers (trapezitai, "table men") took deposits and paid interest. The parable uses the business world of its day as a picture, the way 13:44 uses a man buying a field; it does not teach about lending.

a: Everyone who has something will be given more
t: "Everyone who has will be given more"
p: The same saying as 13:12, about understanding the kingdom.
b: Jesus says the same words about those who receive his teaching (13:12; Mark 4:25; Luke 8:18; Luke 19:26). Those who use what they are given receive more; those who do nothing with it lose it. The sociologist Robert Merton named the way the famous get more credit than the unknown "the Matthew effect" after this verse.

t: The Son of Man on his throne
p: Daniel 7 and 1 Enoch both picture a judge on a glorious throne.
b: Daniel 7:9–14 sets thrones in place for judgment and gives the son of man a kingdom over all peoples. 1 Enoch, a Jewish writing from about Jesus' time, says the kings and the mighty will be seized with pain when they see the Son of Man (in the Ethiopic text, "that Son of a Woman") sitting on the throne of his glory (1 Enoch 62:2–5). Jesus already promised the Twelve that the Son of Man would take his seat on the throne of his glory (19:28). Revelation 20:11–12 shows the dead "standing in front of the throne." Zechariah 14:5, "the LORD my God will arrive, and all the holy ones will be with you," may lie behind "all the angels."

p: All people, or only the nations other than Israel or the church?
b: Panta ta ethnē, "all the nations," is the phrase of the Great Commission (28:19). All humanity: the traditional reading, a picture of the last judgment of everyone, believers included. The Gentiles: some scholars think "the nations" means non-Christian peoples, judged by how they treated Jesus' messengers. Living nations at the start of the millennium: dispensational writers such as Walvoord and Pentecost read this as a judgment of the nations still alive at Christ's return, separate from the final judgment of Revelation 20, and based on how they treated Israel. Note that "them" in Greek is masculine: individuals are separated, not nations as whole countries.

p: Mixed flocks grazed together but were often sorted at night.
b: Shepherds in Israel ran sheep and goats together by day and often separated them in the evening. Ezekiel 34:17 already pictured God judging "between sheep and sheep, between rams and male goats." Sheep were generally the more valuable animals; goats were not evil, but in the picture they stand for those turned away.

t: The Son of Man is the King
p: For the first time Jesus calls himself the King in his own teaching.
b: The Son of Man of 25:31 is now "the King," who speaks of "my Father." Psalm 2 crowns God's Son as king over the nations, and Daniel 7:14 gives the son of man a kingdom. In a few days Jesus will be mocked as "King of the Jews" and crucified under that title (27:29, 37).

a: from the time the world was founded
p: The kingdom was God's plan from the beginning; the fire was not made for people.
b: The kingdom was made ready for the blessed "from the time the world was founded." The fire, by contrast, was made ready "for the devil and his angels" (25:41), not for human beings. Many readers, from the fathers on, have noticed the difference. Compare Ephesians 1:4 and Revelation 13:8.

a: When I was a stranger, you took me in.
p: Jewish teaching already called these the ways to imitate God.
b: Feeding the hungry, clothing the naked and welcoming strangers are commanded in the prophets (Isaiah 58:7; Ezekiel 18:7) and praised in Job 31:16–32 and Tobit 1:16–17. The rabbis taught that to walk after God means to do what God does: he clothed the naked (Adam and Eve), visited the sick (Abraham), and buried the dead (Moses) (Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 14a). Catholic and Orthodox teaching later listed these six acts, plus burying the dead, as the corporal works of mercy.
r: Isaiah 58:7; Ezekiel 18:7; Job 31:16–32; Tobit 1:16–17; Hebrews 13:2–3; James 1:27

a: when did we ever see you hungry
p: Neither the righteous nor the others knew they were meeting the King.
b: The righteous did not help the needy in order to win a reward or even because they knew it was Christ. The others would gladly have served Christ if they had seen him. The surprise on both sides is the point of the scene.

a: one of these brothers of mine, even the least of them
p: Any person in need, or Jesus' own disciples?
b: Any needy person: the most common reading today, behind countless ministries to the poor and much Catholic social teaching. Jesus' disciples: in Matthew, Jesus' "brothers" are his disciples (12:49–50; 28:10), and "little ones" are believers (10:42; 18:6). Whoever takes in Jesus' messengers takes in Jesus (10:40), so the nations are judged by how they treated the poor and persecuted church. Ulrich Luz's history of interpretation finds that most early and medieval readers took the "brothers" to be Christians, and that the universal reading came to dominate in modern times. The Jewish people: some dispensational writers read Jesus' brothers as Jews, or Jewish believers, during the tribulation.

t: Blessed by the Father, cursed by no one named
p: "Blessed by my Father" but simply "cursed": the text does not say who curses.
b: Those on the right are "you whom my Father has blessed" (25:34). Those on the left are simply katēramenoi, "cursed ones," with no "by my Father." Some fathers, and many later readers, saw in this that God is the source of blessing, while people bring the curse on themselves.

p: Prepared for the devil; the same fire as Revelation's lake of fire?
b: Revelation 20:10 shows the devil "thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur." Readers have understood the fire in three main ways. Everlasting conscious punishment: the historic teaching of most churches (Augustine, City of God 21.23). Final destruction: "eternal" describes a result that cannot be undone; the wicked cease to exist (Adventists; some evangelicals, such as John Stott and Edward Fudge). Restoration: some early writers, such as Gregory of Nyssa and Origen, hoped the fire would purify, so that all would finally be saved; a council in 553 condemned the teaching that all surely will. Jude 7 speaks of Sodom's "eternal fire."

p: The same word "eternal" describes the punishment and the life.
b: Aiōnios means "of the age" and is the word in "eternal life", the life of the age to come. Augustine argued that since the same word is used for both, the punishment must last as long as the life (City of God 21.23). Those who hold that the wicked are destroyed say the punishment is eternal in its result. Kolasis once meant pruning or correction, and some, following Origen, read "age-long correction"; by Jesus' time, though, it commonly meant punishment. This is the last sentence of Jesus' teaching in Matthew before the passion.
